before: Assigning another name to a list does not copy the list. Both names can refer to the same object.

Changing a shared object is different from rebinding a local name.
```python
first = ["Moon"]
second = first
second.append("Sun")
print(first)
```
The first name now sees ["Moon", "Sun"] because the object itself changed.
A shallow copy creates a new outer collection but can still share objects nested inside it.

For these nested plain dictionaries and lists, deepcopy makes independent nested copies.
```python
from copy import deepcopy
first = [{"tags": ["sky"]}]
second = deepcopy(first)
second[0]["tags"].append("night")
print(first[0]["tags"])
```
The original tags remain ["sky"]. The copied nested list receives night.
Deep copying is not always necessary or appropriate for every kind of object. Here the contract is ordinary nested list, dictionary, and string data.

after: Assigning another name to a list does not copy it. Both names can use the same list.

Changing a shared list is different from giving a local name a new list.
```python
first = ["Moon"]
second = first
second.append("Sun")
print(first)
```
The first name now sees ["Moon", "Sun"] because the shared list itself changed.
A shallow copy makes a new outside list, but it can still share the items inside. A list or dictionary stored inside another collection is called nested.

For these plain nested lists and dictionaries, deepcopy makes separate nested copies.
```python
from copy import deepcopy
first = [{"tags": ["sky"]}]
second = deepcopy(first)
second[0]["tags"].append("night")
print(first[0]["tags"])
```
The original tags stay ["sky"]. Only the copied nested list gets night.
Deep copying is not always needed or right for every kind of value. Here the data is ordinary nested lists, dictionaries, and strings.
